proofs.proof_tex:
For \(\theta\in\Theta_S\), put \(A_j=\operatorname{supp}(\theta_j)\).  For a prefix \(w\in\prod_{\ell=1}^k\mathcal X_\ell\), define, only within this proof,
\[
q_j^k(w)=\sum_{r_j\in\mathcal R_j}\theta_j(r_j)b_j^k(w,r_j).
\]
The indicator of the event \(\{\operatorname{ev}_{\varnothing}(r)_{\le k}=w\}\) is
\[
\prod_{j=1}^m b_j^k(w,r_j).
\]
Indeed, by acyclicity and the topological order, the prefix is \(w\) exactly when every response equation whose vertex occurs by time \(k\) returns the corresponding coordinate of \(w\); the factors in \(b_j^k\) partition these equations by district.  The product root law in the definition of \(\theta\) therefore gives the prefix factorization
\[
P_\theta(V_{\le k}=w)
=\sum_{r}\prod_{j=1}^m\theta_j(r_j)b_j^k(w,r_j)
=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j^k(w).                                      \tag{1}
\]

Fix \(i\), let \(V_i\in D_j\), and take \((w,a)\in\mathcal F_i(S)\).  Since \(w\in S^{\le i-1}\), there is an \(s\in S\) extending \(w\).  Exact support, as encoded by \(\theta\in\Theta_S\), gives
\[
P_\theta(V_{<i}=w)\ge P_\theta(s)>0.
\]
Equation (1), whose factors are nonnegative, consequently implies \(q_\ell^{i-1}(w)>0\) for every \(\ell\).  For \(\ell\ne j\), no response equation from district \(D_\ell\) is added at step \(i\), and hence
\[
b_\ell^i(wa,r_\ell)=b_\ell^{i-1}(w,r_\ell),
\qquad
q_\ell^i(wa)=q_\ell^{i-1}(w)>0.                                \tag{2}
\]
On the other hand, \(wa\notin S^{\le i}\), so exact support and (1)--(2) give
\[
0=P_\theta(V_{\le i}=wa)
=q_j^i(wa)\prod_{\ell\ne j}q_\ell^{i-1}(w),
\qquad q_j^i(wa)=0.                                             \tag{3}
\]
Every summand in the definition of \(q_j^i\) is nonnegative.  Thus (3) and \(\theta_j(r_j)>0\) for \(r_j\in A_j\) imply
\[
b_j^i(wa,r_j)=0
\quad\hbox{for every }r_j\in A_j.
\]
Since this holds for every first forbidden extension belonging to district \(D_j\), the definition of \(T_j(S)\) yields
\[
A_j\subseteq T_j(S)\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).                       \tag{4}
\]

Now take any \(r\in T(S)\), and write \(v=\operatorname{ev}_{\varnothing}(r)\).  Suppose that \(v\notin S\).  Since \(S^{\le0}=\{()\}\), there is a least \(i\) for which \(v_{\le i}\notin S^{\le i}\).  Then \(v_{<i}\in S^{\le i-1}\), so \((v_{<i},v_i)\in\mathcal F_i(S)\).  If \(V_i\in D_j\), factual evaluation of \(r\) along its own prefix makes every factor in \(b_j^i(v_{\le i},r_j)\) equal to one.  Hence
\[
b_j^i(v_{\le i},r_j)=1,
\]
contrary to \(r_j\in T_j(S)\).  Therefore
\[
\operatorname{ev}_{\varnothing}(T(S))\subseteq S.              \tag{5}
\]

By realizability there is \(\theta^\star\in\Theta_S\).  For each \(s\in S\), the finite sum defining \(P_{\theta^\star}(s)>0\) contains a tuple \(r\) with \(\prod_j\theta_j^\star(r_j)>0\) and \(\operatorname{ev}_{\varnothing}(r)=s\).  Such a tuple belongs to \(\prod_j A_j^\star\), which is contained in \(T(S)\) by (4).  Thus \(S\subseteq\operatorname{ev}_{\varnothing}(T(S))\), and together with (5) this proves
\[
\operatorname{ev}_{\varnothing}(T(S))=S.                       \tag{6}
\]

Let \(\eta_j\) be any mass function strictly positive at every element of \(T_j(S)\), extended by zero to \(\mathcal R_j\setminus T_j(S)\).  Realizability and (4) ensure that every \(T_j(S)\) is nonempty.  Under \(\bigotimes_j\eta_j\), every tuple in \(T(S)\) has positive probability.  Its pushforward support is therefore exactly the image in (6), namely \(S\).  Hence this product law belongs to \(\Theta_S\).  Finally, the response support of any member of \(\Theta_S\) is the Cartesian set \(\prod_j A_j\), and (4) places it inside \(T(S)\), whereas the preceding strictly positive law has response support equal to \(T(S)\).  Thus \(T(S)\) is the unique largest Cartesian response support.

Fix \(\theta\in\Theta_S\), and use the quantities
\[
q_j^k(w)=\sum_{r_j\in\mathcal R_j}\theta_j(r_j)b_j^k(w,r_j)
\]
introduced in the proof of the maximal-response-support theorem.  That proof established
\[
P_\theta(V_{\le k}=w)=\prod_{\ell=1}^m q_\ell^k(w).            \tag{7}
\]
For \(s\in S\), every prefix event in (7) has positive probability because it contains the positive-probability cell \(s\).  Therefore every factor \(q_\ell^k(s_{\le k})\) in (7) is positive.

If \(V_i\in D_j\), then for every \(\ell\ne j\) the district indicator does not change between steps \(i-1\) and \(i\).  Cancelling the positive factors in (7) gives
\[
\frac{P_\theta(V_{\le i}=s_{\le i})}
     {P_\theta(V_{<i}=s_{<i})}
=\frac{q_j^i(s_{\le i})}{q_j^{i-1}(s_{<i})}.                  \tag{8}
\]
The sequence \(q_j^k(s_{\le k})\) changes only at indices \(k\) for which \(V_k\in D_j\).  Since \(q_j^0(())=1\), multiplying (8) over these indices telescopes and yields
\[
\prod_{i:\,V_i\in D_j}
\frac{P_\theta(V_{\le i}=s_{\le i})}
     {P_\theta(V_{<i}=s_{<i})}
=q_j^n(s)
=\sum_{r_j\in\mathcal R_j}\theta_j(r_j)b_j^n(s,r_j).          \tag{9}
\]
By the maximal-response-support theorem, \(\theta_j\) vanishes outside \(T_j(S)\).  The right side of (9) is consequently the \(s\)-row of \(B_j\theta_j|_{T_j(S)}\), while the left side is \(t_j(P_\theta)[s]\).  The normalization row also agrees because both sides equal one.  Hence
\[
B_j\theta_j|_{T_j(S)}=t_j(P_\theta).                            \tag{10}
\]

If \(P_\theta=P_{\theta'}\), definition of \(t_j\) and positivity of all supported prefixes give equality of the right sides of (10), and hence equality of every district signature.  Conversely, factual factorization at a complete supported cell gives
\[
P_\theta(s)=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j^n(s)
=\prod_{j=1}^m (B_j\theta_j|_{T_j(S)})[s],\qquad s\in S.       \tag{11}
\]
Thus equality of all district signatures implies equality of the two laws on \(S\); both laws vanish outside \(S\) by membership in \(\Theta_S\), so they are equal everywhere.

Finally, take arbitrary \(P\in\operatorname{relint}(\Delta(S))\).  If \(s\in S\), then
\[
P(V_{<i}=s_{<i})=\sum_{u\in S:\,u_{<i}=s_{<i}}P(u)\ge P(s)>0.
\]
Every ratio in \(t_j(P)\) is therefore well defined and positive, proving the last assertion without requiring \(P\) itself to be compatible with an SCM.

Let \(\vartheta_j\) denote the column vector \(\theta_j|_{T_j(S)}\).  By the maximal-response-support theorem, all mass of \(\theta\in\Theta_S\) lies on \(T(S)\).  The definitions of the target tensor and the Kronecker matrix therefore give
\[
\tau_{x,y}(\theta)
=h_{x,y}|_{T(S)}\left(\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\vartheta_j\right),
\qquad
B\left(\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\vartheta_j\right)
=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m(B_j\vartheta_j).                            \tag{12}
\]
The matrix \(B\) and vector \(h_{x,y}|_{T(S)}\) have integer entries.  Membership in \(\operatorname{row}_{\mathbb Q}(B)\) is precisely solvability over \(\mathbb Q\) of
\[
\lambda B=h_{x,y}|_{T(S)}.                                     \tag{13}
\]
Multiplying (13) by the product mass vector in (12), and then using the district-signature-recovery theorem, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{x,y}(\theta)
&=\lambda B\left(\bigotimes_j\vartheta_j\right)\\
&=\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\in(\{0\}\cup S)^m}
\lambda[a_1,\ldots,a_m]\prod_{j=1}^m(B_j\vartheta_j)[a_j]\\
&=\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\in(\{0\}\cup S)^m}
\lambda[a_1,\ldots,a_m]\prod_{j=1}^m t_j(P_\theta)[a_j]
=F_\lambda(P_\theta).
\end{aligned}                                                   \tag{14}
\]

It remains to verify the global rational chart.  Every marginal probability appearing in \(t_j(P)\) is a sum of cells \(P(s)\), hence is a polynomial with integer coefficients.  In a fixed product term of \(F_\lambda\), a denominator associated with index \(i\) can occur only in the unique district containing \(V_i\).  If that term uses a supported cell \(a_j\) in that district, the denominator is one of
\[
P(V_{<i}=w),\qquad w\in S^{\le i-1};
\]
if the row is \(0\), no denominator is contributed.  Thus the denominator of each product term divides \(D_S(P)\).  Since \(\lambda\) is rational, bringing the finite sum to the common denominator shows that
\[
F_\lambda(P)=\frac{N_\lambda(P)}{D_S(P)}                       \tag{15}
\]
on the face interior, where \(N_\lambda\) is a polynomial with rational coefficients; cancellation may replace \(D_S\) by a divisor.

For each \(w\in S^{\le i-1}\), choose an \(s\in S\) extending \(w\).  If \(P\in\operatorname{relint}(\Delta(S))\), then
\[
P(V_{<i}=w)\ge P(s)>0.
\]
Every factor in \(D_S(P)\) is consequently positive (the empty-prefix factor is one), so \(D_S(P)>0\) throughout the relative interior.  This proves both the identifying equality and the asserted denominator property.

Write \(E_j=\mathbb Q^{T_j(S)}\) and \(L_j=\operatorname{row}_{\mathbb Q}(B_j)\subseteq E_j\).  Choose a basis of each \(L_j\) and extend it to a basis of \(E_j\).  The resulting tensor-product basis shows directly that
\[
\bigcap_{j=1}^m
\left(E_1\otimes\cdots\otimes E_{j-1}\otimes L_j
\otimes E_{j+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes E_m\right)
=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m L_j.                                       \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, membership in the \(j\)-th space on the left forbids every tensor-basis coordinate whose \(j\)-th factor is outside \(L_j\); membership for all \(j\) leaves exactly the coordinates with every factor in its corresponding \(L_j\).

The rows of a Kronecker product are the tensor products of rows of its factors, so
\[
\operatorname{row}_{\mathbb Q}(B)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m L_j.      \tag{17}
\]
If \(h=h_{x,y}|_{T(S)}\) is outside this space, (16) supplies an index \(j\) for which
\[
h\notin E_1\otimes\cdots\otimes E_{j-1}\otimes L_j
\otimes E_{j+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes E_m.                     \tag{18}
\]
Under the standard coordinate pairing, the annihilator of \(L_j\) is \(\ker(B_j)\).  Hence (18) yields a rational vector \(v\in\ker(B_j)\) such that the contraction
\[
g(r_{-j})=\sum_{r_j\in T_j(S)}h(r_j,r_{-j})v(r_j)              \tag{19}
\]
is not the zero tensor on \(\prod_{k\ne j}T_k(S)\).  The row \(B_j[0,\cdot]\) is the all-ones row, and therefore
\[
\sum_{r_j\in T_j(S)}v(r_j)=0.                                 \tag{20}
\]

For each \(k\ne j\), let \(u_k\) be the uniform probability vector on \(T_k(S)\), and, for \(a\in T_k(S)\), set
\[
\eta_{k,a}=\frac{u_k+e_a}{2}.
\]
These are strictly positive rational probability vectors.  They span \(E_k\), because the matrix having them as columns is
\[
\frac12(I+u_k\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}),
\]
whose determinant is \(2^{-|T_k(S)|}(1+\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}u_k)=2^{1-|T_k(S)|}\ne0\).  Consequently, the pure products \(\bigotimes_{k\ne j}\eta_{k,a_k}\) span \(\bigotimes_{k\ne j}E_k\).  Since \(g\ne0\), there is a selection of indices \((a_k:k\ne j)\) for which
\[
c=\sum_{r_{-j}}g(r_{-j})\prod_{k\ne j}\eta_{k,a_k}(r_k)\ne0. \tag{21}
\]
For \(m=1\), the empty product is one and (21) is simply the nonzero scalar contraction furnished by (19).

Let \(u_j\) be uniform on \(T_j(S)\).  Because \(v\) is rational and \(T_j(S)\) is finite, one can choose a rational \(\delta>0\) satisfying
\[
\delta |v(r_j)|<u_j(r_j)
\quad\text{whenever }v(r_j)\ne0.                               \tag{22}
\]
Define
\[
\theta_j^+=u_j+\delta v,\qquad \theta_j^-=u_j-\delta v,
\qquad
\theta_k^+=\theta_k^-=\eta_{k,a_k}\quad(k\ne j),              \tag{23}
\]
and extend all these vectors by zero off their respective \(T_k(S)\).  Equation (20) makes the two vectors in district \(j\) normalized, and (22) makes every coordinate in (23) strictly positive.  All coordinates are rational.  Moreover,
\[
B_j\theta_j^+-B_j\theta_j^-=2\delta B_jv=0,                   \tag{24}
\]
and the signatures in every other district agree because the laws there are identical.  The maximal-support theorem puts both product laws in \(\Theta_S\), and district-signature recovery together with (24) gives
\[
P_{\theta^+}=P_{\theta^-}.                                    \tag{25}
\]
Finally, (19)--(23) give
\[
\tau_{x,y}(\theta^+)-\tau_{x,y}(\theta^-)=2\delta c\ne0.     \tag{26}
\]
Only the \(j\)-th district law differs, which proves every assertion.

The equality
\[
\operatorname{row}_{\mathbb Q}(B)
=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\operatorname{row}_{\mathbb Q}(B_j)
\]
follows because the rows of \(B=\bigotimes_jB_j\) are exactly the tensor products of rows of the factors; their rational span is the tensor product of the individual rational row spans.

If \(h_{x,y}|_{T(S)}\) belongs to this row space, the rational-functional theorem supplies a single function \(F_\lambda\) such that
\[
\tau_{x,y}(\theta)=F_\lambda(P_\theta)
\quad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_S.
\]
Therefore equal observational laws imply equal target values, which is uniform identification.

Conversely, if the tensor is outside the row space, the rational-interior-twins theorem supplies \(\theta^+,\theta^-\in\Theta_S\) with
\[
P_{\theta^+}=P_{\theta^-}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\tau_{x,y}(\theta^+)\ne\tau_{x,y}(\theta^-).
\]
This pair violates the defining same-law implication for uniform identification.  The two alternatives are exhaustive, proving the equivalence.

For the diagonal bow, let \(U\) be a fair binary root for its single district.  In the first SCM set
\[
X=U,\qquad Y=U,
\]
and in the second set
\[
X=U,\qquad Y=X.
\]
Both structural assignments respect \(G_{\mathrm{bow}}\), both have factual law assigning probability \(1/2\) to each element of \(S_{\mathrm{diag}}\), and neither assigns mass outside that support.  Under \(\operatorname{do}(X=1)\), however,
\[
P(Y=1)=\frac12
\quad\text{in the first SCM},
\qquad
P(Y=1)=1
\quad\text{in the second SCM}.                                \tag{27}
\]
Thus the query is not uniformly identified.  By the uniform-identification tensor-span theorem, the tensor criterion rejects it.  This also shows explicitly why the factual equality \(Y=X\) on the diagonal support cannot be substituted after intervention.

For the five-cell instrumental-variable control, the districts are \(\{Z\}\) and \(\{X,Y\}\).  Write a downstream response type as
\[
(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1),
\]
where \(x_z\) is the response of \(X\) to \(Z=z\), and \(y_x\) is the response of \(Y\) to \(X=x\).  Applying the first-forbidden-prefix conditions to \(S_{\mathrm{IV5}}\) gives exactly the following downstream saturated types:
\[
\begin{array}{cc}
(0,0,0,0),&(0,0,0,1),\\
(0,1,0,1),&(1,0,0,0),\\
(1,0,1,0).&
\end{array}                                                     \tag{28}
\]
To verify (28), when \(z=0\), factual support permits \((x,y)=(0,0)\) and \((1,0)\), forcing \(y_0=0\) if \(x_0=0\) and \(y_1=0\) if \(x_0=1\).  When \(z=1\), it permits \((0,0),(0,1),(1,1)\), imposing no restriction on \(y_0\) if \(x_1=0\) and forcing \(y_1=1\) if \(x_1=1\).  Combining the four possibilities for \((x_0,x_1)\) yields precisely the five types in (28), with the case \((1,1)\) impossible because it would require both \(y_1=0\) and \(y_1=1\).

Inspection of (28) gives the pointwise response identity
\[
\mathbf 1\{y_0=1\}
=\mathbf 1\{x_1=0,\ y_{x_1}=1\}.                              \tag{29}
\]
The left side of (29) is the outcome indicator under \(\operatorname{do}(X=0)\).  The right side is the indicator of \(\{X=0,Y=1\}\) under \(\operatorname{do}(Z=1)\).  The root for \(Z\) is independent of the downstream root, so conditioning factually on \(Z=1\) leaves the downstream root law unchanged.  Because \(S_{\mathrm{IV5}}\) contains cells with \(Z=1\), exact support gives \(P(Z=1)>0\).  Taking expectations in (29) therefore yields
\[
P_{\operatorname{do}(X=0)}(Y=1)
=P_{\operatorname{do}(Z=1)}(X=0,Y=1)
=P(X=0,Y=1\mid Z=1).                                          \tag{30}
\]
Thus this query is uniformly identified and the tensor criterion accepts it by the equivalence theorem.  Equation (30), including its positive conditional denominator, is the asserted five-cell functional.

Finally, suppose \(S=\mathcal X_V\) and a query is classically identified for \(G\).  By the meaning of classical identification, any two graph-compatible SCMs having the same observational law have the same query value.  This implication applies in particular to the canonical independent-district-root subclass \(\Theta_S\).  Uniform identification on this exact full-support face follows, so the tensor criterion accepts the query.  On every positive graph-compatible law, the classical functional and the rational functional supplied by the rational-functional theorem both equal the same interventional target; hence they agree there.  No equality away from the graph-compatible observational model is required.

Let \(d=|S|\), and regard the simplex as a subset of \(\mathbb R^d\).  On
\[
K_\epsilon=\left\{p\in\Delta(S):\min_{s\in S}p(s)\ge\epsilon\right\},
\]
every supported prefix probability is at least \(\epsilon\): for a prefix \(w\in S^{\le i-1}\), choose an extending cell \(s\in S\) and use \(p(V_{<i}=w)\ge p(s)\).  The rational representation in the rational-functional theorem therefore has denominators uniformly bounded away from zero on a relative neighborhood of \(K_\epsilon\).  Since the dimension is finite, \(F_\lambda\) has uniformly bounded first and second derivatives on a slightly larger compact neighborhood, for example wherever all cell probabilities are at least \(\epsilon/2\).

Write
\[
g_P(s)=\frac{\partial F_\lambda(P)}{\partial P(s)}.
\]
The definition of \(\phi_P\) gives \(\phi_P(s)=g_P(s)-\sum_uP(u)g_P(u)\), and hence \(\sum_sP(s)\phi_P(s)=0\).  If \(a:S\to\mathbb R\) is any score in the saturated multinomial tangent space, so that \(\sum_sP(s)a(s)=0\), the path \(P_t(s)=P(s)\{1+t a(s)\}\) satisfies
\[
\left.\frac{d}{dt}F_\lambda(P_t)\right|_{t=0}
=\sum_s g_P(s)P(s)a(s)
=\sum_s\phi_P(s)P(s)a(s).                                     \tag{31}
\]
Every mean-zero function on \(S\) is such a tangent direction.  Thus \(\phi_P\) is the unique mean-zero representer of all pathwise derivatives in the saturated multinomial tangent space, and hence is the efficient influence function.  Its variance is \(\sigma^2(P)\) by definition.

Let
\[
E_N=\left\{\|\widehat P_N-P\|_\infty\le\epsilon/2\right\}.
\]
The multinomial variance formula and a union bound with Chebyshev's inequality give
\[
\sup_{P\in K_\epsilon}P(E_N^c)
\le \frac{4d}{N\epsilon^2}.                                   \tag{32}
\]
Moreover, the event that some supported cell is unobserved has probability at most
\[
\sum_{s\in S}\{1-P(s)\}^N\le d e^{-N\epsilon}.                \tag{33}
\]
On its complement, \(D_S(\widehat P_N)>0\), so the plug-in definition equals \(F_\lambda(\widehat P_N)\).  On \(E_N\), the uniform second-derivative bound and Taylor's theorem give
\[
F_\lambda(\widehat P_N)-F_\lambda(P)
=\sum_{s\in S}g_P(s)\{\widehat P_N(s)-P(s)\}+R_N,
\qquad
|R_N|\le C\|\widehat P_N-P\|_2^2,                             \tag{34}
\]
where \(C\) is independent of \(P\in K_\epsilon\).  Because the empirical masses sum to one, the linear term in (34) is
\[
\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N\phi_P(O_k).                               \tag{35}
\]
Also \(\sup_P E_P[N\|\widehat P_N-P\|_2^2]\le d\), so (32)--(34) imply \(\sqrt N R_N=o_P(1)\) uniformly.  Together with (33), this proves the asserted uniform asymptotic linear expansion for \(\widehat\tau_N\).

On \(\mathcal P_{S,\epsilon,\underline\sigma}\), bounded first derivatives and \(\sigma(P)\ge\underline\sigma\) imply a constant \(M<\infty\) such that
\[
\left|\frac{\phi_P(s)}{\sigma(P)}\right|\le M
\quad\text{for all }s\in S
\quad\text{and all }P\in\mathcal P_{S,\epsilon,\underline\sigma}. \tag{36}
\]
For any sequence \(P_N\) in this class, the triangular array
\[
W_{N,k}=\frac{\phi_{P_N}(O_k)}{\sqrt N\,\sigma(P_N)},
\qquad k=1,\ldots,N,
\]
has independent mean-zero entries, total variance one, and satisfies the Lindeberg condition by (36).  The cited Lindeberg--Feller theorem therefore gives
\[
\frac1{\sqrt N\,\sigma(P_N)}\sum_{k=1}^N\phi_{P_N}(O_k)
\rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,1).                              \tag{37}
\]
If convergence in (37) were not uniform over the class, a violating sequence \(P_N\) could be selected, contradicting (37).  Hence the convergence is uniform.

Define \(v(p)=\sum_sp(s)\phi_p(s)^2\) wherever the prefix denominators are positive.  The same compact-neighborhood derivative bounds make \(v\) uniformly continuous near \(K_\epsilon\).  Equations (32)--(33) and uniform consistency of \(\widehat P_N\) consequently imply
\[
\sum_{s\in S}\widehat P_N(s)\phi_{\widehat P_N}(s)^2
-\sigma^2(P)=o_P(1)                                            \tag{38}
\]
uniformly, on the event where the displayed plug-in expression is defined; defining it arbitrarily on the complement does not change (38) because that complement has uniformly vanishing probability by (33).  The variance lower bound and (38), followed by the uniform version of Slutsky's argument, turn (34)--(37) into uniform convergence of
\[
\frac{\sqrt N\{\widehat\tau_N-F_\lambda(P)\}}
{\left\{\sum_s\widehat P_N(s)\phi_{\widehat P_N}(s)^2\right\}^{1/2}}
\]
to \(\mathcal N(0,1)\).  Finally, on the compatible submodel, the rational-functional theorem gives \(F_\lambda(P_\theta)=\tau_{x,y}(\theta)\), so the same expansion and studentization provide Wald inference for the causal target rather than merely for an observed-law functional.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(W_{q,1},\ldots,W_{q,k_q}\) be a triangular array of independent real random variables with mean zero.  If \(\sum_{i=1}^{k_q}\operatorname{Var}(W_{q,i})\to1\) and, for every \(\delta>0\),
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k_q}\mathbb E\!\left[W_{q,i}^2\mathbf 1\{|W_{q,i}|>\delta\}\right]\longrightarrow0,
\]
then \(\sum_{i=1}^{k_q}W_{q,i}\rightsquigarrow\mathcal N(0,1)\).

source.locator: Theorem 2.27 (Lindeberg--Feller central limit theorem), specialized to one dimension

attestation.note: The exact theorem locator and stable DOI are supplied; the proof uses only the one-dimensional variance-one specialization.

proposed.statement: Fix a successful certificate \(\lambda\). In the saturated multinomial model on \(S\), \(\phi_P\) is the efficient influence function of \(F_{\lambda}(P)\). Under independent multinomial sampling, uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_{S,\epsilon,\underline\sigma}\), \(\sqrt N\{\widehat\tau_N-F_{\lambda}(P)\}=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^N\phi_P(O_k)+o_P(1)\), the studentized statistic converges uniformly to \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), and the plug-in variance \(\sum_{s\in S}\widehat P_N(s)\phi_{\widehat P_N}(s)^2\) is uniformly consistent. On the compatible submodel this gives Wald inference for \(\tau_{x,y}\).
proposed.justification: A complete symbolic identifier becomes statistically usable once its rational output has face-tangent inference.
proposed.gap: Bhattacharya, Nabi, and Shpitser derive graph-native influence functions for important functional classes, but not for arbitrary rational outputs created by exact-support identification on a lower-dimensional multinomial face.
proposed.consumer: Analysts with known structural zeros obtain standard errors and confidence intervals without replacing the deterministic intervention target.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the classical triangular-array central limit theorem that is the sole published asymptotic premise used in the proof.

open_obligations.what_is_open: A finite syntax of do-search states and an explicit list of signed, support-scoped transition rules whose derivations normalize to the tensor certificate, together with a simulation of every tensor row-space elimination by those rules.
open_obligations.obstruction: The frozen compiler handle specifies semantic invariants and a desired normalization but does not define a transition relation, rule side conditions, expression encoding, or cancellation discipline. Consequently termination and rule-by-rule soundness are not well-typed properties of the present handle, and neither a completeness proof nor a finite counterexample to an unspecified calculus can be given.
open_obligations.attempted: The support-saturated response sets, positive-prefix district signatures, commuting rootwise row-space projections, rational Gaussian elimination, and signed tensor identity were compiled into a finite semantic decision procedure. What remains is a bidirectional simulation between a concrete do-search grammar and these tensor operations; in particular, signed products of district signatures must retain intervention scopes through cancellation.
open_obligations.partial_result: The semantic tensor compiler is finite and complete: let \(K=(|S|+1)^m\), \(M=|T(S)|\), and \(r=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}(B)\).  Enumeration of the finite sets \(T_j(S)\), formation of \(B\), and rational Gaussian elimination decide whether \(h_{x,y}|_{T(S)}\in\operatorname{row}_{\mathbb Q}(B)\).  On success, one may choose \(r\) independent rows and a nonsingular \(r\)-by-\(r\) minor, obtaining a certificate \(\lambda\) with at most \(r\le\min\{K,M\}\) nonzero entries.  Cramer's rule and Hadamard's inequality bound the numerator and denominator of each reduced coefficient by \(r^{r/2}\), hence its bit length by \(O(r\log r)\).  The resulting functional has denominator dividing \(D_S(P)\).  On failure, the one-district rational perturbation in the rational-interior-twins theorem is a finite exact nonidentification certificate.  This proves a bounded, sound, and complete response-tensor decision procedure, but it does not prove that a specified do-search transition system realizes that procedure without materializing the tensor.
